title: Carbon Markets, Green Credit and LiFE

cards.b:
India has built three connected instruments: a compliance carbon market, the Green Credit Programme and Mission LiFE. They are fresh in the news and ideal for Mains.

Keep them separate in your mind: one prices carbon, one rewards land and nature actions, one changes behaviour.

A compliance market sets a legal limit or intensity target for firms. Those who beat it earn credits and sell to those who miss. A voluntary market lets firms buy credits to offset their emissions.

Two designs: cap-and-trade (absolute cap, as in the EU ETS, started 2005) and baseline-and-credit (intensity targets). India uses the intensity model.

The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 allowed carbon markets. The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified in 2023 and its rules sit with the Ministry of Power. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency is the administrator, the Grid Controller of India is registry, and CERC regulates trading.

It replaces the earlier PAT energy efficiency scheme (2012). One credit equals one tonne of CO2e.

Intensity targets for 2025–26 and 2026–27 have been notified in stages for energy-intensive sectors including aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper, and later petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and others (as of 2026; reports differ on counts of units). Targets have been notified for nine sectors (power is excluded); trading was targeted to begin around October 2026.

An offset mechanism also allows non-obligated projects, such as renewables and afforestation, to earn credits.

The Green Credit Rules were notified under the Environment Protection Act in October 2023. It is voluntary and market-based, and the administrator is ICFRE, Dehradun. At COP28 India launched the Green Credit Initiative.

Eligible activities include tree plantation, water conservation, sustainable agriculture, waste management, air pollution reduction, mangrove restoration, Ecomark and sustainable building. People or firms can earn a credit and trade it.

LiFE was announced by the Prime Minister at COP26 (2021) and launched on 20 October 2022 at Kevadia, Gujarat with the UN Secretary-General. It promotes simple habits: saving energy and water, cutting waste and plastic, eating sustainably and adopting healthy lifestyles.

It builds Pro-Planet People and treats behaviour as a climate tool, backed by India’s case that overconsumption in rich countries is a cause.

The Paris Agreement’s Article 6 allows international transfer of credits (6.2) and a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4). Rules agreed at COP29 (2024) open the way for India’s credits to be sold abroad, with safeguards against double counting.

India will need to match domestic CCTS rules with Article 6 accounting.

Carbon markets can fail through weak baselines, double counting and low prices. Intensity targets may not cap total emissions. Green Credit has been criticised for treating nature like a commodity and for land tied up in plantations.

Supporters say markets mobilise private money and reward early action, and are better than rules alone.

India’s industry is energy-intensive and exports face the EU CBAM from 2026. A domestic carbon price could help exporters show they already pay a price for carbon.

The three tools fit the NDC goals and the 2070 net-zero target.

CBAM, the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, taxes imports of carbon-intensive goods such as steel, cement, aluminium and fertiliser, with a transition period that began in 2023 and charges that follow later. Indian exporters worry about competitiveness. A domestic carbon price may reduce the amount payable abroad. India has also objected that CBAM breaks the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.

Mains-style: “What is the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme? How does it differ from PAT and from the Green Credit Programme?” Structure: definitions; legal base; sector coverage; differences (compliance versus voluntary, industry versus nature); risks; way forward.

Prelims tip: CCTS: BEE as administrator. Green Credit Administrator: ICFRE. LiFE launched 2022. EU ETS began 2005.

Answer pointers: the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 gave the legal basis for a carbon market. CCTS uses emission intensity targets for covered entities, unlike absolute caps in the EU ETS. The Green Credit Programme rewards voluntary actions such as tree planting and water conservation, so it is not a compliance market. Do not mix PAT energy savings certificates with carbon credits. Mention double counting and price discovery as risks.

quiz.q: The administrator of India’s Green Credit Programme is:
quiz.w: Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education.

quiz.q: India’s carbon market is mainly based on:
Which Act enabled carbon markets in India?
quiz.w: It gave power to set a carbon credit scheme.
An energy efficiency trading scheme from 2012.

quiz.q: The EU Emissions Trading System began in:
Article 6 of the Paris Agreement concerns:
quiz.w: 6.2 and 6.4 relate to transfers and a UN crediting mechanism.

quiz.q: A Green Credit can be earned by:
Which regulator oversees trading of carbon credits in India?
